name: Polypharmacy and Deprescribing
rawContent:
# Polypharmacy and Deprescribing

## 1. OVERVIEW
Polypharmacy (commonly defined as ≥5 regular medications) increases risk of adverse drug events, falls, hospitalisation and medication-related morbidity in older people. Deprescribing is the process of supervised medication withdrawal to minimise harm and improve outcomes.

## 2. RECOGNITION
Identify patients with many regular medicines, recent falls, cognitive impairment, recurrent lines of adverse drug reactions or hospital admissions. Use tools: STOPP/START, Beers criteria, medication review checklists, anticholinergic burden scales.

## 3. INVESTIGATION
Full medication reconciliation (including OTC and herbal), check indications, durations, interactions, renal/hepatic function, and patient goals of care. Assess frailty, cognition and life expectancy when weighing benefits vs harms.

## 4. MANAGEMENT
Conduct structured medication review: prioritise deprescribing of drugs with limited benefit, high risk (e.g., anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, long-term opioids, proton pump inhibitors without indication), and those causing orthostatic hypotension. Use shared decision-making, taper where needed, monitor withdrawal effects, and document rationale. Consider involvement of pharmacist and geriatrician.

## 5. FOUNDATION DOCTOR ROLE
Perform medication reconciliation, flag high-risk patients for formal review, start deprescribing under supervision for simple items (e.g., stop duplicate therapies, review PPI indications), and arrange follow-up to monitor for symptom recurrence or withdrawal.

overview.definition: Use of multiple medicines leading to increased risk of harm; deprescribing is supervised withdrawal to reduce risk.
overview.epidemiology: Very common in older adults and those with multimorbidity; prevalence rises with age and care complexity.
overview.pathophysiology: Increased adverse drug events (ADEs), drug-drug interactions, falls, cognitive impairment, hospital admissions, and reduced quality of life due to cumulative burden of multiple medications.

signs: Recent medication changes correlating with symptom onset
redFlags: Recent falls or syncope after new medication
High anticholinergic burden in frail elderly

firstLine: Comprehensive medication reconciliation (including OTC and herbal)
Beers criteria for potentially inappropriate medications
secondLine: Renal function (U&E, eGFR) for dose adjustments
Liver function tests if hepatic metabolism relevant
Review drug levels if applicable (e.g., digoxin, phenytoin)

diagnosis.criteria: Polypharmacy is typically defined as use of ≥5 regular medications. Problematic polypharmacy occurs when the risks outweigh benefits, or when medications lack clear indication or duplicated therapy exists.

firstLine: Stop/withhold suspected causative medication if acute harm (e.g., AKI, delirium)
Review and rationalise medications in acutely unwell patients
secondLine: Involve clinical pharmacist for urgent medication review

firstLine: Structured medication review using STOPP/START or similar tools
Identify and stop medications without clear ongoing indication
Taper drugs requiring gradual withdrawal (benzodiazepines, opioids, antidepressants, PPIs)
monitoring: Monitor for withdrawal effects or symptom recurrence after deprescribing
Regular follow-up to assess safety and tolerability
Communication with primary care and all prescribers

clinicalPearls: Common deprescribing targets: long-term PPIs, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, anticholinergics in dementia, duplicate antihypertensives.
Always taper benzodiazepines, opioids, antidepressants, and PPIs gradually to avoid withdrawal.
Use 'start low, go slow' when initiating new drugs in older adults.
Beware of prescribing cascades: treating side effects of one drug with another drug.
content.prognosis: Successful deprescribing reduces adverse events and can improve quality of life without worsening disease control in many cases.
content.foundationDoctorRole: Identify and document medication issues, start simple deprescribing under supervision, communicate changes to primary care, and ensure monitoring plans are in place.
content.escalation: Refer to clinical pharmacist or geriatrician for complex polypharmacy, high-risk medications, or when deprescribing expertise is needed.
content.keySafetyConsiderations: Ensure gradual tapering of high-risk drugs; monitor for withdrawal effects; communicate all changes clearly to patient, carers, and GP; arrange follow-up.
